title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
statement:
Build a class `RandomizedCollection` that keeps a multiset of integers (one value may be stored several times). Each operation must take O(1) time on average.

- `RandomizedCollection()` starts with an empty collection.
- `insert(val)` stores one more copy of `val`, whether or not copies are already there. It returns `true` if the collection held no copy of `val` before the call, and `false` otherwise.
- `remove(val)` deletes exactly one copy of `val` and returns `true` when a copy exists; when none exists it changes nothing and returns `false`.
- `getRandom()` returns a randomly chosen stored item in which every stored copy is equally likely, so a value with `c` copies among `s` items comes back with probability `c / s`. It is only called while the collection is non-empty.

Because `getRandom` is random, the judge accepts any value that is currently stored, and on long runs of `getRandom` calls it also checks that each value appears roughly as often as its share of copies.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls in total are made to insert, remove and getRandom
The collection holds at least one item whenever getRandom is called
notes:
## Intuition

A random pick in O(1) needs the items packed in an array: choose a random index and read it. Removing from the middle of an array is slow, though, unless we fill the hole with the last item and pop the end. To find a copy of `val` to remove without scanning, keep a map from each value to the set of indices where its copies sit. The brute-force alternative, `indexOf` plus `splice`, costs O(n) per removal.

## Approach

1. `values` holds every stored copy; `positions` maps a value to the `Set` of its indices in `values`.
2. `insert`: create the value's set if needed, add the next index, push `val`, and return whether the set now has exactly one index.
3. `remove`: if `val` has no set, return `false`. Otherwise take any `index` from its `slots` and drop it.
4. Move the last item, `lastValue`, into `index`; in its set add `index` first, then delete `lastIndex`, and pop the array.
5. If `slots` became empty, delete `val` from the map so the next insert reports `true`.
6. `getRandom`: read `values` at a uniformly random index; a value with more copies owns more indices.

## Example 1, step by step

- `insert(1)`: `values = [1]`, `positions = {1: {0}}`, returns `true`.
- `insert(1)`: `values = [1, 1]`, `{1: {0, 1}}`, returns `false`.
- `insert(2)`: `values = [1, 1, 2]`, `{1: {0, 1}, 2: {2}}`, returns `true`.
- `getRandom()` picks one of three indices, so 1 with probability 2/3 and 2 with probability 1/3.
- `remove(1)`: `index = 0`, `slots = {1}`; the last item 2 moves to index 0, its set becomes `{0}`, and the pop leaves `values = [2, 1]`. Returns `true`.
- `getRandom()` now returns 2 or 1 with equal chance.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) on average per call: map and set operations are hashed, and the array only changes at its end.
- Space: O(n) for the array and the index sets.

## Pitfalls

- Add `index` to the last value's set before deleting `lastIndex`; when the removed copy is the last item, the two are equal and the order makes the net change correct.
- Delete empty sets from the map, or `insert` will report `false` for a value that is gone.
- A plain list of indices per value would need a linear search to remove `lastIndex`; a `Set` does it in O(1).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `values` | every stored copy, packed with no holes |
| `positions` | value → set of its indices in `values` |
| `slots` | the index set of the value being inserted or removed |
| `index` | the slot being emptied by `remove` (or picked by `getRandom`) |
| `lastIndex`, `lastValue` | the final position of `values` and the item there |
| `lastSlots` | the index set of `lastValue` |
